enrichment.short_title: Begum jilbab school uniform and Article 9 challenge
key_facts: Shabina Begum, a 15-year-old Muslim pupil at Denbigh High School, Luton, wore the approved Shalwar Kameeze uniform for two years before insisting from September 2002 on wearing a jilbab.
The school refused entry unless she complied with the published uniform policy, which had been developed after consultation with parents and mosques.
She did not attend school thereafter; the school maintained she was not excluded and offered compromise arrangements including a modified Shalwar Kameeze.
She sought judicial review alleging unlawful exclusion and breaches of Articles 9, 2 Protocol 1 and 14 ECHR.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive claim for judicial review of Denbigh High School's refusal to allow attendance in a jilbab; permission against Luton Borough Council refused.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review claim against the school dismissed; no breach of Article 2 Protocol 1 found; permission to proceed against the local education authority refused.
enrichment.ratio: A published school uniform policy limiting Muslim girls to an approved Shalwar Kameeze rather than a jilbab was a clear, proportionate limitation on Article 9 rights necessary for the proper running of a multi-faith secular school and protection of others' rights; the pupil was not excluded and her Article 2 Protocol 1 right to education was not denied where she could comply with uniform or seek transfer.
legal_issues: Whether refusal to admit a pupil in a jilbab amounted to unlawful exclusion
Whether the uniform policy infringed Article 9 ECHR
Whether Article 2 Protocol 1 was breached by denial of education
Whether the limitation was prescribed by law, pursued a legitimate aim and was proportionate

enrichment.short_title: Council liability for refusing window safety catch
key_facts: A two-year-old child fell from a first-floor casement window of a council house let by Blaenau Gwent, sustaining serious injury.
The tenant had previously asked the council to fit window locks or safety catches after a near-miss involving an older child; the council refused on fire-safety policy grounds.
The trial judge held the council liable by analogy with Stockley for failing to give individual consideration to the request.
After the accident the council fitted a restrictor catch that would have prevented the fall.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by the local authority against a finding of common law negligence despite no disrepair and no occupier's liability duty.
enrichment.ratio: A landlord council with no duty in respect of the condition of premises is not liable in negligence for refusing window locks requested on fire-safety grounds where the tenant sought locks rather than safety catches, no assumption of responsibility arose, and Stockley is distinguishable as involving a duty to abate an external hazard in an emergency.
legal_issues: Whether a council landlord owed a duty of care to fit child-proof window safety devices
Application of Stockley v Knowsley MBC
Whether blanket fire-safety policy required individual exception
Distinction between locks and safety catches

enrichment.short_title: Somalia asylum judicial review on risk on return
key_facts: Mustafa Adam, an Ashraf clan member from Somalia, claimed asylum after family members were killed in 1995 and he received protection from Sheikh Abdi of the majority Marehan clan.

The adjudicator accepted clan membership and residence in Somalia but found he had integrated into Marehan protection, left for economic reasons and faced no well-founded fear of persecution on return.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused permission to appeal in May 2003; judicial review was not lodged until February 2004.
Ground 9 alleged the adjudicator failed to address current risk on return to Somalia.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review of IAT refusal of permission to appeal against an asylum dismissal, heard long out of time.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no error of law in the adjudicator's determination or the tribunal's refusal of permission.
enrichment.ratio: Where an adjudicator expressly finds that a claimant had Marehan protection, was no longer at risk as a minority clan member and could return to that protection, the risk-on-return issue is sufficiently addressed even if not labelled separately; absence of an arguable point of law bars judicial review.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator failed to make findings on current risk on return
Whether membership of a minority clan remained relevant after Marehan integration
Whether the IAT erred in refusing permission to appeal
Effect of significant delay in bringing judicial review

enrichment.short_title: Margam Forest wind farm section 288 challenge
key_facts: Community Power Ltd appealed unsuccessfully to the National Assembly for Wales against refusal of permission for eleven wind turbines at Margam Forest on Mynydd Margam.
The inspector found serious harm to Margam Park, scheduled monuments, a registered historic landscape and the Llangynwyd Conservation Area outweighed renewable-energy benefits.

Whether Policy EQ7 applied to a non-statutory historic landscape designation

enrichment.short_title: Unduly lenient sentence for hammer assault in pub
key_facts: The offender attacked a stranger in a hotel bar with a claw hammer over a trivial jukebox dispute, striking three blows to the head after leaving and returning to the premises.
The victim suffered a depressed skull fracture with dura breach requiring titanium plates, lasting neurological and psychological effects and loss of employment.
He pleaded guilty to wounding with intent on the day of trial; the judge sentenced him to three years' imprisonment.
The Attorney General referred the sentence as unduly lenient.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 Criminal Justice Act 1988 following a late guilty plea at Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Reference upheld; sentence increased from three years to four and a half years after double-jeopardy allowance.
enrichment.ratio: An unprovoked public hammer attack on an innocent stranger causing serious lasting head injury, with multiple blows and continued aggression, merited a sentence of about five and a half to six years before allowance for a late guilty plea and double jeopardy; three years failed adequately to mark gravity and deter similar violence.
legal_issues: Whether three years' imprisonment was unduly lenient for s18 wounding with intent
Weight to be given to late guilty plea and personal mitigation

enrichment.short_title: Unfair dismissal for falsifying banking records

statutes_considered.title: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992

key_facts: Chris Kelly, a regional operations manager with 22 years' service at Anglian Home Improvements, was dismissed for gross misconduct including falsifying daily banking records on the JDE system.
He recorded monies as banked before receipt to reduce branch debt figures and meet targets, despite a clear May 2001 memo requiring daily banking.
A split Employment Tribunal majority treated the conduct as figure massaging insufficiently serious for dismissal; the chairman dissented.
The Employment Appeal Tribunal upheld the dismissal decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer's appeal against EAT dismissal of its appeal from a split Employment Tribunal unfair-dismissal finding.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Kelly's unfair dismissal claim dismissed without remittal.
enrichment.ratio: The lay members substituted their personal view for the band of reasonable responses test; deliberate falsification of banking records plainly constituted gross misconduct under the employer's disciplinary code, and on the facts found no reasonable tribunal could conclude dismissal was outside the range of reasonable responses.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal applied the band of reasonable responses test
Whether split extempore tribunal reasons were adequate
Whether the employer's disciplinary procedure and ACAS Code were properly considered
Whether perversity justified final dismissal of the claim without remittal

enrichment.short_title: Listed gatehouse link extension planning challenge

statutes_considered.title: Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990

key_facts: Mr Thompson sought planning permission and listed building consent to link two Grade II gatehouses at the Cannon Hall estate, Barnsley, into a single dwelling.
Council officers had recommended approval but the council refused after parish council objection; the inspector dismissed both appeals finding harm to listed buildings and landscape value.
The claimant renovated the unused South Lodge believing consent would be granted, creating an appearance of recent occupation.
The inspector treated the lodge as ancillary accommodation in active use, affecting the PPG15 balancing exercise.

enrichment.outcome: Claims allowed; inspector's decisions quashed and matter remitted for fresh determination; claimant awarded £600 costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where an inspector materially misapprehended that a listed gatehouse was in recent active use when renovations were done in expectation of consent, and that error could have affected the PPG15 justification balancing exercise, the decision must be quashed even if the same outcome might have been reached on correct facts.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector erred in finding the South Lodge was in use
Whether failure to call council officers prejudiced the informal hearing
Whether economic viability and PPG15 justification were adequately addressed

enrichment.short_title: Violent disorder appeal on identification direction
key_facts: Simon Hassan was convicted of violent disorder after acquittal on three wounding-with-intent counts arising from a 2002 school-area fight between Bengali and Afghan youths.
Prosecution case relied on witnesses identifying him by a black Avirex jacket and Moschino jeans rather than facial recognition.
